term_types.name: Tokenised traditional asset status
term_types.question: Is the crypto-asset a digital representation of a traditional asset (bond, equity, deposit, commodity, cash in custody) conferring the same legal rights and risk as the traditional form?
term_types.description: Basel treats tokenised traditional assets as Group 1a only if they confer the same legal rights and credit and market risk as the traditional asset. The US PWG report and CFTC treat tokenised securities as regulated by the underlying asset rather than the technology.

coverage_notes: Omitted as ungrounded or too thin: a separate 'native token versus token' dimension was folded into crypto_asset_base_chain_architecture as a single-source reading. Dimensions for AI-enabled crime, DPRK-specific laundering methods, and DeFi exploit vectors appear only as event descriptions in docs 18-19 and were not treated as classification criteria. Dimensions about market metrics (price, volatility, TVL, market share, market capitalisation rankings) were excluded by the taxonomy paper and by the DLT-Corpus, which use them as descriptive statistics rather than classification criteria. Scientific and patent document-volume analyses in doc 3 and the sentiment labels were not classification criteria. Sections 1, 2, 4 of doc 3 and the introduction sections of doc 1 contain background rather than classification criteria. The FATF 2021 section on stablecoin governance and central-body status (doc 17) was used only in the notes of stablecoin dimensions. The UN Convention (doc 23) and Budapest Convention (doc 24) define property and computer data generically and contribute only the 'virtual assets as property' definition and a freezing/seizure definition, which is cited under obligation_or_risk_sanctions_and_freezing_capability. The Basel definitions section (doc 20, SCO60.131) was used for the operator, redeemer and validator roles, which are cited in actor-level notes. The EU AMLR and transfer regulation definitions were used for actor and activity dimensions. The UK SI 2026/102 interpretation section (doc 8, regulation 2) only defines Regulated Activities Order cross-references. Sections of doc 1 on security and privacy and on the component taxonomy's Gossiping, Latency, and Finality were used only for technology dimensions where cited. The 2026 Clarity Act Senate substitute (doc 10) and the 2025 House-passed Clarity Act (doc 11) overlap in definitions and were both used where they differed.
